items.summary: Loop invariants are essential for deductive program verification, yet automatically inferring them for {multiphase programs}, whose loops contain conditional branches that induce multiple execution phases with distinct behaviors, remains an open problem. Existing LLM-based methods either reason about loops as a whole or use explicit branch information to generate atomic assertions jointly across branches, without maintaining complete candidate sub-invariants for independent generation and targeted repair. We present CLOVER, a structured neurosymbolic reasoning framework for multiphase invariant inference built on two interlinked mechanisms. First, compositional inference: CLOVER statically decomposes a loop into symbolic {loop branch sequences}, conjunctions of the loop guard and branch conditions that characterize distinct execution scenarios, and guides the LLM to generate candidate sub-invariants for each one independently, so that each LLM query focuses on a single execution scenario rather than the entire loop. Second, counterexample-guided localized refinement: when SMT verification rejects a composed disjunctive invariant, CLOVER traces the counterexample back through the branch structure to identify which specific loop branch sequence caused the failure and repairs only that sub-invariant, preserving all correct components. Both mechanisms are unified by a shared symbolic structure derived from the loop's branch semantics, which guides what the LLM generates, how candidates are composed, and where refinement is directed. We evaluate CLOVER on 316 linear arithmetic, 50 nonlinear arithmetic, and 54 multiphase benchmarks. CLOVER solves 35 of 54 multiphase benchmarks, outperforming the best LLM-based baseline (29) by 20.7\% and the best traditional method (22) by 59.1\%. On linear/nonlinear benchmarks, CLOVER remains competitive, solving 355 of 366 programs overall.
items.title: Compositional Loop Invariant Inference for Multiphase Programs via Structured Neurosymbolic Reasoning

items.summary: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
items.title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models

items.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is increasingly used in settings where pairwise preferences coexist with pointwise criteria such as response length, answer correctness, or safety scores. When the two disagree, standard DPO treats pairs whose preferred output scores worse on the pointwise criterion (conflict pairs) in the same way as the remaining (matching) pairs. We characterize a systematic failure mode, constraint drift: for sufficiently small updates, conflict pairs tend to increase constraint cost while matching pairs tend to repair it, and the net change depends on their balance. This balance yields a closed-form pre-alignment diagnostic, $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$, computable from dataset statistics, that indicates whether a dataset is self-correcting or requires intervention. Building on this diagnostic, we propose Conflict-aware DPO (CoDPO), which down-weights conflict pairs with a strength set from $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ rather than tuned, and adds an adaptive margin shift that addresses residual drift during training. Empirically, drift grows monotonically with conflict exposure on the conflict-dominated domains, and the intervention decision given by $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ matches the observed drift on every domain, including one that it identifies as self-correcting. On all four domains of the main comparison, CoDPO reduces drift while largely preserving the preference learning of vanilla DPO. Compared with hard filtering and recent constrained and multi-objective baselines, CoDPO also achieves a more favorable drift-preference trade-off.
items.title: When Scores Conflict with Preferences: Pre-Alignment Diagnosis and Adaptive Correction of Constraint Drift in DPO

items.summary: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/
items.title: Seeing Beyond the Next Step: World-Model-Guided Human-Like Navigation in Multi-Agent Scenes

items.summary: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.
items.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness

items.summary: Language agents increasingly use persistent memory to record user preferences and procedures across sessions. We show that memory from benign interactions can cause unsafe or unreliable behavior on later tasks. We call this failure the memory trap. To study this issue, we compare behavior in sessions with and without memory across six frontier models (including Claude Sonnet, Opus, and Fable models and GPT-5.6). We evaluate these models in a range of settings. First, in autonomy experiments, we find that requests to skip confirmation during low-stakes coding chores lead agents to skip confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks in both coding and everyday life. We next study memories formed when users seek emotional support, or describe harm from uncritical feedback, and find these memories bias later judgments of mathematical work, arguments, and poems toward sycophancy or over-critique (respectively). Memory notes written during legitimate stale-test repairs lead agents to weaken correct tests that catch broken safeguards; these memories also increase cheating on ImpossibleBench, with larger increases for stronger Sonnet and Opus models. We show that memory traps can arise both from overgeneralizations in memory writing, and when acting on memory. These findings demonstrate that even benign interactions can lead to serious risks from memory systems, and thus motivate the need for new research into ensuring that agents preserve the scope of their memories.
items.title: The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions

items.summary: The goal of these notes is to provide a unified and rigorous introduction to robust sequential decision-making. We offer a self-contained introduction to the main results in the field. After a concise introduction to MDPs we introduce robust MDPs with general uncertainty sets, before focusing on rectangular models of uncertainty. We make a significant effort to show connections between robust MDPs and several other popular models for sequential decision-making: MDPs with uncertain rewards, Multi-Objective MDPs and Pareto optimality, MDPs with time-varying uncertain parameters, non-rectangular robust MDPs, stochastic games, distributionally robust MDPs, and risk-averse MDPs. Having all these results in one place, within a single unifying formalism, will hopefully be useful for researchers who want to start working on this topic. The exposition combines operator and fixed point approaches, convex optimization (more specifically, duality in saddle-point problems), and game-theoretic arguments. The latter identifies robust MDPs with a certain type of two-player game; this helps build useful intuition, especially when constructing counterexamples.
items.title: Robust Markov Decision Processes: An Introduction Using Convex Optimization and Game Theory

items.summary: Proportional fair (PF) scheduling in fifth-generation (5G) New Radio (NR) ranks user equipment (UE) by instantaneous rate over an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) of delivered service. We identify a served-but-undelivered denial-of-service (DoS) attack in which rank indicator (RI) inflation induces persistent physical resource block (PRB) starvation. Unsupported spatial layers cause first-attempt delivery failure, keeping the attacker's service EWMA low; the evaluated PF allocator repeatedly grants it the full PRB pool, denying honest UEs transmission opportunities. We formalize this recurrence and evaluate it in 3,300 paired, 200 slot multi-user shards spanning rank 1 and rank 2 Sionna Ray Tracing geometries, three link adaptation controllers, PF and round robin (RR), four target identities, and five seeds. On the rank 2 geometry, selective RI inflation yields 94--95\% target capture, reduces PRB Jain fairness from 0.997 to 0.28, and produces mean honest zero-grant runs of 41--56\,ms; RR preserves equal allocation. Exact offline replay and a Monte Carlo recurrence isolate the delivered-service denominator as the causal path. Cross-field and controller ablations show a weaker, controller-dependent channel-quality trigger, while activity-gated EWMA defenses remain structurally blind. The results motivate RI-consistency checks before feedback acquires scheduling authority and slot-time PRB evidence inside the O-RAN Distributed Unit.
items.title: PRB Starvation at Slot Time via Rank Indicator Inflation: Attacking Proportional Fair Memory in the Scheduler

items.summary: BackgroundAn outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) occurred in young people from Catalonia (Spain) who travelled to Menorca (Spain) in summer 2021. This outbreak appeared when governments relaxed Covid-19 preventive measures: the mask usage and the opening of nightlife. It was related to a super-disseminating mass event: Sant Joan festivities in Ciutadella. The aim of this article is to describe an outbreak of COVID-19 in young people aged 17-19 years from Catalonia travelling to Menorca. MethodsThis is an observational study of a COVID-19 outbreak. The study population comprised Catalonian youth aged 17-19 years who travelled to Menorca from 15 June to 10 July. Epidemiological descriptive indicators were obtained. Descriptive and geographical statistics were carried out. Bivariate Moran's I test was used to identify spatial autocorrelation between the place of residence and deprivation. The outbreak control method was based on identifying and stopping chains of transmission by implementing the test-trace-isolate-quarantine (TTIQ) strategy. ResultsWe identified 515 confirmed cases infected in Menorca, 296 (57.5%) in girls and 219 (42.5%) in boys, with a total of 2,280 close contacts. Of them, 245 (10.7%) were confirmed as cases. The cases were diagnosed between 15 June and 10 July. None of the persons with confirmed infection died or required hospitalisation. The attack rate was 27.2%. There was an inverse relationship between deprivation and number of confirmed cases (p<0.005), there were clusters of confirmed cases in the most socioeconomic favoured areas. DiscussionThe outbreak is related with young people from socioeconomic favoured areas who travelled to Menorca in summer 2021. Failure to comply with preventive measures in binge-drinking events and during holidays may have favoured SARS-CoV-2 transmission. The interauthority coordination and establishment of a clear line of leadership allowed continuous communication between institutions, which were key to managing this complex COVID-19 outbreak.
items.title: A large outbreak of COVID-19 linked to an end of term trip to Menorca (Spain) by secondary school students in summer 2021

items.summary: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.
items.title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?

items.summary: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.
items.title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance

items.summary: Training an agent to play Pac-Man with only up, down, left and right actions raises a basic question: when performance is poor, what should be improved? Difficulty can arise from reading the screen or from choosing actions over a long sequence. We examine these problems in a Qwen3.5-9B-based agent through separate perception checks and primitive-policy reinforcement-learning studies. In the policy study, which uses textual boards to remove image transcription from the decision interface, completion on eight held-out mazes increased from 0% before this optimization to 80.2% at a selected checkpoint, with three extra lives. The perception checks show that accurate static screenshot reading can coexist with errors during interaction. A separate policy comparison also shows that further optimization can accompany worse action choices. Together, these findings motivate concrete checks for post-training: evaluate perception in use, distinguish training success from full-game validation, and examine decisions and later performance rather than relying on one selected score. The study provides empirical lessons for improving future agent training and evaluation.
items.title: Where It Breaks: Diagnosing Perception, Memory, and Decision Failures of a Vision-Language Agent in Pac-Man

items.summary: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.
items.title: MAC-v2: Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels

items.summary: v2.1.0 - Current Microbiology corrected reproducibility analysis Study: Cohort-conditioned portability of microbiome biomarkers in Parkinson's disease and colorectal cancer. Parkinson's disease analysis This release provides the corrected three-cohort analysis using 675 public microbiome profiles: 148 from Finland, 200 from Malaysia and 327 from the United States. The conservative genus-label representation contains 154 matched labels, with 46 descriptive features. Outer-fold and cohort-held-out AUROCs: | Model | Pooled | Cohort-held-out | |---|---:|---:| | ElasticNet | 0.731206 | 0.679606 | | Random Forest | 0.741901 | 0.626226 | | XGBoost | 0.716056 | 0.619658 | Cohort-associated variation exceeded disease-associated variation. The results support a measurable average portability gap, with performance varying across held-out cohorts. Independent score evaluation The independent simulation experiment separates coefficient fitting, strategy selection and evaluation using disjoint source donors. The selected six-component ElasticNet score was constant and failed independent discrimination (AUROC 0.50). The proposed categorical portability rule and clinical-probability interpretation are not validated by these results. Heterogeneity alone and alternative scoring strategies are reported for comparison. Colorectal cancer benchmark The contextual CRC analysis includes 1,850 samples, 12 studies and 668 MSP features. Pooled out-of-fold AUROC: 0.725096. Concatenated study-held-out AUROC: 0.689825. Unweighted mean study AUROC: 0.704407. CRC-specific recalibration is not presented as independent validation of the PD score. Sequencing quality control Authentic observed-ASV rarefaction curves are provided for all 675 PD samples. Finland: 148 samples. Malaysia: 200 samples. United States: 327 samples. 64 seeded without-replacement replicates per sample. The release includes per-sample curves, cohort summaries, raw-run accession mappings, processing provenance, QC tables and SHA256 checksums. The sequencing-QC processing did not alter the frozen classifier inputs or fitted models. Reproducibility This release includes corrected processed inputs, sample-level provenance, analysis scripts, model outputs, statistical tables, figures, independent score-evaluation results and executable reproduction instructions. The previous v2.0.0 release remains available as the earlier analysis version. Its numerical results should not be used as the current study results. No raw FASTQ files are redistributed.
items.title: squareshorts/pd-microbiome-portability: v2.1.0 - Current Microbiology corrected reproducibility analysis

items.summary: The growing adoption of digital pathology has rapidly expanded collections of hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images, yet efficient navigation through these archives remains challenging, as metadata is often inconsistent or unavailable. Content-based image retrieval addresses this challenge by identifying similar cases directly from visual representations instead of manual annotations or metadata. Existing retrieval systems have demonstrated promising performance but largely rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, constraining scalability and generalization. Here, we present CLEAR-WSI (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) as a scalable, diagnostic-driven slide-retrieval framework, validated on both public and clinical data. Using a fixed-length slide embedding, CLEAR-WSI refines retrieved candidates with either a predicted diagnostic label or the ground-truth label, depending on the retrieval setting. Newly processed cases are subsequently added to the expanding memory bank, allowing the retrieval archive to grow over time. On a comprehensive benchmark consisting of two public and one private clinical datasets representing four retrieval tasks, CLEAR-WSI improves Precision@5 over the strongest evaluated baseline, with gains on CAMELYON16 (3.10), BRACS-1 (2.75), BRACS-2 (1.95), and X-HER2 (3.75). Additional ablation and latency studies further examine the contribution of each component and highlight its potential for scalable deployment.
items.title: Towards Scalable Diagnostic-Driven Whole-Slide Image Retrieval for Pathology Archives

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.
items.title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?

items.summary: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.
items.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration

items.summary: Proving an alternating-current optimal power flow solution globally ε-optimal usually takes a convex-relaxation solve per instance. Most of these solves can be reused. For a fixed multiplier, the box-constrained Lagrangian bound of a conic relaxation is affine in the load, so a multiplier computed once gives a lower bound at every load by an inner product. Where the relaxation's prices vary smoothly in few load directions, packing numbers in their number bound the size of a library from above and, under a curvature assumption, from below, and solving the relaxation only where the library falls short stays within the upper bound; where prices are constant within operating regimes, one multiplier per regime suffices. On eight benchmark systems of 14 to 500 buses, one multiplier per regime certifies nearly as many loads as a thousand, and a library used first makes an interior-point-plus-relaxation pipeline 3.0 to 15.2 times faster at ε = 0.5%, depending on the baseline configuration, and 8.9 times while proving both bounds. Grown this way over a year of hourly loads of a modified 2000-bus Texas grid, a library certified 98.2% of the hours with 252 solves.
items.title: Amortized and Rigorous Optimality Certificates for AC Optimal Power Flow via Load-Affine Dual Libraries

items.summary: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.
items.title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery

items.summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents translate model outputs into consequential actions, turning indirect prompt injection into an execution-security problem. Existing defenses constrain tool calls, trajectories, or information flows, but often leave action semantics, state dependencies, and evidence relations implicit, limiting generalization across heterogeneous tools and complicating safe updates. We present \ours{}, a dynamic ontology-guided governance framework. \ours{} grounds heterogeneous calls in a shared semantic representation and combines an executable ontology with episode-level task state to derive deterministic ready, waiting, and forbidden decisions. A waiting decision identifies an unmet but recoverable obligation, enabling bounded replanning without expanding the agent's authorization boundary. \ours{} evolves its ontology offline from verified training executions. An offline LLM proposes instance-independent action--state axioms, which are accepted only if they address ontology errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen. We evaluate \ours{} on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn under benign and indirect prompt-injection settings. \ours{} achieves a 0\% attack success rate (ASR) across all three benchmarks while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines. These results show that explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking.
items.title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents

items.summary: We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks. LifeVal covers the most valuable life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate, representing over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories (e.g., managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, finding childcare). To construct our activity distribution, we conducted a new survey of willingness-to-pay for a digital superassistant across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referencing our results against the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) and the Multinational Time Use Study (Fisher et al., 2025). For the most valuable consumer activities, we recruited task creators to create AI evaluation tasks personalized using real ChatGPT conversations and memories, reference files, and personal context. Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year) and also write a rubric, ensuring that our evaluation measured the best personalized completion for that task. All tasks had to pass at least three rounds of human quality-control before acceptance into our final evaluation sets.
items.title: LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks

items.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly involved in both producing and evaluating scholarship, raising fundamental questions about how editorial judgments should be documented, contested, and governed. Existing publication models offer complementary approaches to access, selection criteria, review visibility, and preservation, yet these dimensions must be specified independently when evaluative work is delegated to AI systems. This inaugural editorial/perspective introduces the Journal of Autonomous Scholarship (JAS), a fee-free, open- access, multidisciplinary journal welcoming human-authored, AI-assisted, and AI-generated manuscripts under a uniform standard of evidential support, methodological or logical validity, clarity, and research integrity. JAS combines seven explicitly identified AI editorial roles and two revision-continuity auditors with publicly reusable review instructions, hash-bound review provenance, a mechanical and substantive acceptance gate that blocks unresolved material objections, author proof verification, and named human administrative oversight. To support inspection, we assemble a dated companion archive containing local source files, policy and handbook documents, machine-readable prompts and schemas, a synthetic serialization fixture, and extracted historical review reports. The archive is embedded in the supplement PDF; reviewer access does not depend on a separately uploaded ZIP. A file-hash manifest identifies the local snapshot; its equivalence to the previously cited repository commit and the original runtime environment has not been established. We distinguish normative policy requirements, implemented software controls, and prelaunch verification limits, examine risks arising from correlated model errors, non-execution of code during text-based review, and single-publisher governance, and specify a prospective benchmark agenda with finding- and manuscript-level error metrics and cluster-robust uncertainty estimation. AI-reviewed by the Journal of Autonomous Scholarship. Authenticated submitting researcher: 0000-0002-6249-7193. AI disclosure: See manuscript Data/code: See manuscript Funding and conflicts: See manuscript Ethics: See manuscript
items.title: Introducing the Journal of Autonomous Scholarship: Scope, Editorial Architecture, and a Vision for Accountable AI Publishing

items.summary: This archive accompanies "Diffusivity-uniform mean corrections and initial-layer memory in a thermochemical reaction-diffusion-ODE system" by Nam-Hyun Yoo, Hyojin Park and Jinhong Yang. It provides reproducible numerical benchmarks for the diffusivity-uniform quadratic mean correction and the composite fast-diffusion expansion with initial-layer memory. Supplementary Code S2 contains two-dimensional periodic calculations with 39 primary nonlinear trajectories: 25 at beta=3 and 14 at beta=20. It includes equal-variance wavelength comparisons, numerical controls, the mean-conversion timing-source decomposition at D=1 and D=64, and the high-activation composite comparison at D=64 for all seven saved amplitudes. Independent adjoint/quadrature and saved-array checks accompany the results. The supplied AA_Supplementary_Note.pdf is identical to the Supplementary Note supplied with the manuscript. Sections 1-8 and 11.3-11.4 describe S2. Sections 9-10 and 11.1-11.2 describe the one-dimensional and closed-form results in Supplementary Code S1, version 1.1.2: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23993893. The note's LaTeX source and required figures are included. README.txt and MANUSCRIPT_MAP.txt describe the correspondence with manuscript Sections 5.5-5.6 and its figures and tables. Version 1.0.3 updates the title, citations, documentation and module docstrings and includes the current Supplementary Note. Existing numerical files, original figure files and executable Python statements are unchanged from version 1.0.2, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23789502. The release history is retained in CHANGELOG.txt. Python source code, including comments and docstrings, is licensed under MIT. Data, figures, configurations and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Pinned dependencies, reproduction commands and SHA-256 checksums are included. The results are deterministic mathematical benchmarks. Funding: National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA), funded by the Korea government (MSIT), grants RS-2026-25621689 and RS-2026-25621708.
items.title: Supplementary Code S2: Two-dimensional and high-activation verification for Diffusivity-uniform mean corrections and initial-layer memory in a thermochemical reaction-diffusion-ODE system

items.summary: A child who learns to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace the difference to what a learner reads when it decides. A position, a count or a time keeps taking new values as the input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine is at least 99% correct, on average over lengths 41 to 500, on nine of fifteen benchmark tasks, five of them tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves; given new cycles after training it reverses strings of 15,015 symbols without error and fails beyond that on the curve the theory predicts; and its controllers run unchanged on neurons.
items.title: How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer

items.summary: In the context of Industry 4.0, predictive maintenance is essential to minimize unplanned downtime and ensure operational safety. In machining processes, drill jamming is a critical failure that compromises both workpiece quality and tool integrity. This work proposes an acoustic anomaly detection system using ultrasonic sensors to identify pre-failure patterns in Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining. We release a public dataset of time- and frequency-domain acoustic features from 17 drills, and benchmark semi-supervised autoencoder-based normality modelling against supervised XGBoost classification using Leave-One-Drill-Out validation. The results demonstrate that the Autoencoder is highly effective for industrial safety, achieving a Recall of 1.00 and a consolidated F1-score of 0.81. Furthermore, the threshold-independent analysis shows that the Autoencoder better separates normal and pre-failure acoustic patterns, achieving a consolidated AUC of 0.8294, compared with 0.7559 for the supervised model under inter-tool covariate shift. In contrast, the supervised XGBoost achieved an average F1-score of 0.55 and failed to detect failures in some of the evaluated drills. The findings highlight that the ultrasonic spectrum provides a reliable window for identifying incipient mechanical instabilities, and the AE model offers a robust safety envelope by anticipating all jamming events across the tested drill bits.
items.title: Acoustic Anomaly Detection for Early Identification of Drill Jamming

items.summary: This archive accompanies "Diffusivity-uniform mean corrections and initial-layer memory in a thermochemical reaction-diffusion-ODE system" by Nam-Hyun Yoo, Hyojin Park and Jinhong Yang. items.summary: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
items.title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models

items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
items.title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge

items.summary: The continuous expansion of digital infrastructure, especially data centers, has imposed unprecedented, geographically concentrated stress on existing power grids. However, rigorous causal evidence quantifying how these facilities reshape local power-infrastructure supply remains limited. This study builds a comprehensive county-level US panel dataset spanning 2010-2024, uniquely integrating individual data center building footprints and power-plant additions. To mitigate endogeneity and high-dimensional confounding, this study deploys Double Machine Learning with five-fold cross-fitting, conditioning on county and year fixed effects alongside regional socioeconomic covariates. Baseline estimation identifies a significant positive causal effect robust across multiple rigorous specifications. The result holds following 1%-99% winsorization that downweights mega-clusters including Loudoun County: growth in data-center floor area drives meaningful increases in nearby power-generation capacity (ATE=1.982, P=0.000, CI: [1.25, 2.72]). Outcomes remain statistically significant using a one-year lagged treatment to address reverse causality, and are stable under state-level fixed-effect alternatives. An event-study framework augmented with historical agglomeration controls validates clear parallel trends and detects a sharp causal spike at t = 3, matching typical utility-scale grid-construction lead times. A placebo test further verifies these causal estimates cannot emerge from random chance. Substantial regional heterogeneity emerges: strong positive impacts concentrate in the West, while significant negative displacement-related effects appear within resource-constrained Northeastern counties. These results deliver timely insights for urban planners and energy regulators, stressing the importance of forward-looking grid-capacity investment to support ongoing digital transformation.
items.title: Data Center Agglomeration and Power Infrastructure Capacity in the United States

items.summary: This paper proposes the Transient-Loss Functional Compounding Theory (TLFCT), a medium-independent, time-indexed framework for investigating how a temporary loss in a system's functional performance may be associated with subsequent capability formation, recovery, net gain, and, under more restrictive conditions, compounding improvement. The central proposition is conditional rather than universal: a transient functional loss can contribute to a positive long-term outcome when a demonstrable conversion mechanism produces retained adaptive capacity or another relevant functional resource, and when the resulting future net benefit is sufficient to offset the initial loss and additional costs. The framework distinguishes transient loss, recovery, compensation, positive net conversion, and functional compounding. It proposes explicit measures for the initial loss, future benefit, subsequent degradation, additional costs, net outcome, loss-to-gain ratio, net conversion index, and break-even time. It also introduces a candidate state-space architecture connecting disturbance, information, feedback, adaptive capacity, performance, and resource constraints. The proposed theoretical architecture contains eighteen analytical layers and nine cross-cutting research modules. Its methodological foundation combines dynamical systems, systems theory, cybernetics, information theory, statistical model selection, and causal inference. A primary case design, a real-time measurement protocol, eight research hypotheses, a falsification strategy, a cross-domain validation plan, and a fourteen-stage research roadmap are specified. TLFCT is presented as a proposed research framework, not as an empirically established universal law. Its mathematical specifications are candidate models whose applicability, identifiability, predictive performance, and domain-level invariance must be established through empirical research.
tags: transient functional loss; adaptive capacity; net functional gain; functional compounding; dynamical
items.title: The Transient-Loss Functional Compounding Theory (TLFCT)

items.summary: IntroductionResilience is considered of high relevance when developing interventions to cope with stressful situations. Schools are one of the key settings to promote resilience among adolescents. The purpose of this cluster randomized controlled trial is to assess the effectiveness of an intervention in adolescents at risk, aged 12-to-15 years old, to increase resilience and emotional regulation strategies.MethodsThe recruitment period started in January 2022. Schools will be randomly allocated to control and intervention groups by an external researcher using computer-generated random numbers. The minimum sample size was estimated to be 70 participants per group. Primary health care nurses will carry out the intervention during the school period (January to June 2022). Students will follow a specific training consisting of six 55-min sessions, for 6 weeks. Each session will consist of 5 min of mindfulness, followed by 45 min of the corresponding activity: introducing resilience, self-esteem, emotional regulation strategies, social skills, problem-solving, community resources, social and peer support, and 5 min to explain the activity to do at home. Data will be collected at baseline, 6 weeks, and 24 weeks after the intervention. The child youth resilience measure-32 (CYRM-32) scale will be used to assess the effectiveness of the intervention. This study received a grant in June 2021.DiscussionThe intervention is intended to improve mental health through resilience. Different factors related to resilience will be promoted, such as self-esteem, emotional regulation, social and communication skills, problem-solving and peer support, among others. As it has been designed as a cluster-randomized school-based intervention, we will directly ameliorate the participation and engagement of the target population. With the present intervention, we expect to improve coping skills in adolescents by enhancing resilience capacities. Copyright © 2023 Llistosella, Torné, García-Ortiz, López-Hita, Ortiz, Herández-Montero, Guallart, Uña-Solbas and Miranda-Mendizabal.
items.title: Fostering Resilience in Adolescents at Risk: Study protocol for a cluster randomized controlled trial within the resilience school-based intervention

items.summary: Introduction: Basic life support training in school age is a topical issue because, with adequate training, any person can help save a life.Methods: Cluster clinical trial with data collection through an ad hoc self-administered, semi -structured questionnaire. The target population encompassed the students aged 4--6 years enrolled in 49 educational centres. The centres were randomly allocated to the intervention or control group. The intervention group was trained with the RCParvulari (R) methodology, consisting of theoretical and practical training on the first link of the chain of survival. The control group only received theoretical training. We evaluated participants before and immediately after the intervention and between 3 and 12 months post-intervention by means of the ques-tionnaire. We assessed the acquisition and retention over time of the knowledge and skills covered in the training compared to previous trainings in both groups.Results: A total of 1327 schoolchildren (79% of the target population) participated. The level of knowledge acquired immediately after training and after 3-12 months compared to baseline was significantly better (P <.001) in the intervention group than in the control group, both in early recognition and contacting of emergency services (112) and in remembering the "mouth -nose-eyes " mnemonic.Conclusions: The RCParvulari (R) methodology significantly contributed to an improved ability to recognize a possible medical emergency, start the chain of survival by alerting an adult and call the 112 emergency number in students in the last year of preschool education.
items.title: RCParvulari training: A basic life support training methodology applied to 5-year-old students: Effectiveness in a cluster-randomized clinical trail

items.summary: Offline reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on a fixed pool of sampled responses and typically supervises every token of every response, although responses and tokens are not equally informative. We study which ones to supervise through the Gibbs-optimal policy of KL-regularized RLVR, which offline training targets, and measure the mismatch between a policy and this target with a bidirectional KL divergence. At the reference policy, this mismatch factorizes exactly and separates the two outcomes: correct responses contribute mainly through the forward term, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and incorrect responses through the reverse term, concentrated on the responses the policy generates often and on their high-probability tokens. Based on this analysis, we propose GIST (Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection), a two-level selection method that approximates these principles with signals available before training. GIST uses the sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy's mode, and it uses the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies. Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises the average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP for all three models under both objectives. In a controlled comparison on Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.
items.title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR

items.summary: This deposit contains the data and the analysis code that reproduce the Methods and Results of a systematic review of polymer-based dental materials incorporating an engineered self-healing mechanism. The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework on 26 October 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QCZFY) before formal screening and before any data were extracted. The review separates three contrasts that the literature conflates under the single heading of healing efficiency: C-I, the baseline penalty of the self-healing material in its virgin state against a capsule-free control; C-II, the recovery of the repaired material against the same material in its virgin state; and C-III, the net position of the repaired material against a conventional material without a healing system. The effect measure is the log ratio of means, back-transformed to a ratio and a percentage. Contents. The extraction matrix holds 105 arm-level rows covering four studies and 17 harmonised outcomes, each row linked to the exact formulation of both arms, the source page and the provenance of the value. Four further tables record the full-text eligibility decisions for the 48 assessed reports, the re-screening of the 96 discarded reports against the registered criteria, the characteristics of the studies carrying extracted data, and the register of 16 departures from the registered protocol. The R pipeline recomputes the 89 arm-level contrasts, the three pre-specified contrasts, the efficient-frontier criterion, both manuscript figures and the main and supplementary effect tables. A validation script asserts 21 reported values and halts the pipeline on any mismatch. Reproduction. R 4.4 or later with the metafor package is the only requirement. Running "Rscript run_all.R" from the root of the package regenerates every output in a few seconds and writes a session record alongside them. Limits of these data. Sixty of the 105 rows derive wholly or partly from provisional single-reader readings of figure panels and were not validated by duplicate digitisation; the provenance columns identify them. Five contrasts have a mean of zero in the numerator or the denominator, so the ratio of means is undefined for them. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were not assessed. Arm-level data were extracted from four of the 39 included studies. Licensing. Data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; the code under R/, run_all.R and legacy/ is released under the MIT Licence.
items.title: Self-healing dental polymers: extraction matrix and analysis code for a systematic review with endpoint harmonisation

items.summary: Serving large language models (LLMs) under tight memory and latency service-level objectives (SLOs), including on edge devices, requires jointly selecting the model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and mixed-precision quantization recipes. Exhaustive search over this combinatorially large space is infeasible. Unlike data-center serving, which often prioritizes throughput or generation speed, resource-constrained deployments typically set memory and latency budgets as constraints and then seek the configuration with the highest generation quality among feasible ones. To this end, we propose ACSeL, a framework that identifies configurations predicted to satisfy deployment constraints while achieving high predicted generation quality. To enable efficient quality estimation, we use Relative Model Quality Degradation (RMQD), a proxy based on the divergence between the candidate and reference models' next-token distributions over a small calibration corpus. Across the evaluated model sizes and precisions, RMQD is inexpensive to evaluate and strongly correlated with downstream benchmark performance. ACSeL combines (i) a lightweight quality surrogate that predicts RMQD directly from a configuration; (ii) Few-shot Median Calibration (FMC), which calibrates operator-profile-based latency estimates using a small number of end-to-end profiles; and (iii) a structured search algorithm BandPareto for exploring layerwise mixed-precision configurations. Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge platform show that FMC substantially improves deployment feasibility, while BandPareto + FMC achieves the highest feasibility and the lowest RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations in the evaluation set.
items.title: ACSeL: Adaptive Configuration Search for Hardware-Constrained LLM Inference

items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.
items.title: TACT-KV: Tri-Axis Cosine Transform for Compressing Volumetric KV Caches in Medical VLMs

items.summary: PREPRINT SUBMITTED TO RENEW 2026 CONFERENCE.   MoodyMarine is an open-access weakly nonlinear potential flow solver for wave-body and mooring interactions. In this study the capabilities of MoodyMarine for modeling tension-leg-platform (TLP) type floating offshore wind turbines (FOWT) is assessed. A TLP-type platform has been simulated for four wave cases of increase wave steepness and compared to experimental data measurements of surge, heave, pitch, and mooring-line tension. A qualitatively and quantitatively comparison has been carried out using the root-mean-square error (RMSE), the relative root-mean-square-error (RRMSE), and the correlation coefficient (R). A numerical calibration was carried out for the baseline wave condition showing that the required initial experimental mooring stiffness had to be reduced from K = 132N/mm to K = 50N/mm to ensure good agreement between experimental and numerical data. Pitch motion agreement improved significantly (88.4 % reduction in RRMSE), while surge responses experienced small variations since surge is dominated by wave excitation rather than tendon stiffness. Mooring line tensions showed only a small improvement, as the baseline tension errors were already low. For the rest of the validation cases MoodyMarine showed good agreement with the experimental data while keeping the computational time to 0.152 s of CPU time per 1 s of simulated time.
items.title: NUMERICAL VALIDATION OF A FLOATING OFFSHORE WIND TLP-TYPE PLATFORM USING MOODYMARINE

items.summary: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.
items.title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors

items.summary: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
items.title: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models

items.summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
items.title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

items.summary: Proportional fair (PF) scheduling in fifth-generation (5G) New Radio (NR) ranks user equipment (UE) by instantaneous rate over an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) of delivered service. We identify a served-but-undelivered denial-of-service (DoS) attack in which rank indicator (RI) inflation induces persistent physical resource block (PRB) starvation. Unsupported spatial layers cause first-attempt delivery failure, keeping the attacker's service EWMA low; the evaluated PF allocator repeatedly grants it the full PRB pool, denying honest UEs transmission opportunities. We formalize this recurrence and evaluate it in 3,300 paired, 200 slot multi-user shards spanning rank 1 and rank 2 Sionna Ray Tracing geometries, three link adaptation controllers, PF and round robin (RR), four target identities, and five seeds. On the rank 2 geometry, selective RI inflation yields 94--95\% target capture, reduces PRB Jain fairness from 0.997 to 0.28, and produces mean honest zero-grant runs of 41--56\,ms; RR preserves equal allocation. Exact offline replay and a Monte Carlo recurrence isolate the delivered-service denominator as the causal path. Cross-field and controller ablations show a weaker, controller-dependent channel-quality trigger, while activity-gated EWMA defenses remain structurally blind. The results motivate RI-consistency checks before feedback acquires scheduling authority and slot-time PRB evidence inside the O-RAN Distributed Unit.
items.title: PRB Starvation at Slot Time via Rank Indicator Inflation: Attacking Proportional Fair Memory in the Scheduler

items.summary: Code, data and outputs that reproduce a study of carbon embodied in China–EU trade and of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The archive covers three analyses: (1) CO2 embodied in China–EU27 trade, 2011–2022, from a global multi-regional input–output model (EXIOBASE 3.9.6, with release 3.8.2 for reconciliation and sensitivity); (2) China's potential CBAM certificate costs, 2026–2034; (3) EU27 imports from higher- and lower-carbon origins after CBAM reporting began, using a PPML triple-difference design on monthly Eurostat Comext data, January 2018 to July 2026. It contains the Python, R and Stata code, the analysis panel, derived input–output results, CBAM parameter files, codebooks, download manifests with checksums, and the output tables, figures and logs. The EXIOBASE 3.9.6 carbon multipliers and the ICAP daily price data are not included, in line with the source licences; the code to rebuild or process them is provided. Start with README_replication_archive.md. Code is released under the MIT licence and data under CC BY-SA 4.0 or CC BY 4.0, as set out in LICENSE.md.
items.title: Replication archive: Embodied CO2 in China–EU trade and early responses to the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism

items.summary: Who Drops Out? Replication data and code Data and code for the article "Who Drops Out? A National Analysis of Dropout Rates in Indonesian Higher Education" (Alvin Armein, Universitas Sumatera Utara; under review). The study links two public PDDikti datasets for academic year 2024 (registered students and student dropouts) for 31,170 study programs at 3,811 institutions, and estimates adjusted dropout rate ratios with Poisson models. Contents Path Description analysis_cells.csv.gz Linked analysis dataset: one row per study program x sex x age band (268,392 rows), institutions anonymised program_level.csv The same data summed to one row per study program, with dropout rates CODEBOOK.md Column definitions and data sources Supplementary_Who_Drops_Out.xlsx Supplementary tables S1–S21: rates, all models, anonymised program-level data code/ Python scripts that build the dataset, fit the models and draw the figures (see code/README.md ) Anonymisation Institution names, national institution codes (NPSN) and districts are not included. Each institution has a random ID (INST-0001 ...), the same in all files. Source data Kementerian Pendidikan Tinggi, Sains, dan Teknologi, Pusat Data dan Teknologi Informasi (2025): Registered students: https://data.kemdiktisaintek.go.id/dataset/data-jumlah-mahasiswa-tahun-2025 Student dropouts: https://data.kemdiktisaintek.go.id/dataset/data-jumlah-mahasiswa-drop-out-tahun-2025 The original ministry files are not redistributed here; download them from the links above to rerun code/ .
items.title: Who Drops Out? Replication data and code

items.summary: Study-Specific Replication Instructions for Study 1 from Nancekivell, Shah, & Gelman (2020): “Maybe they’re born with it, or maybe it’s experience: Toward a deeper understanding of the learning style myth.” Journal of Educational Psychology, 112 (2), 221-235. DOI of original article: https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/edu0000366 Briefly, the steps you take to complete a CREP replication of this project are: Sign up , and wait to get your project number and related information. Follow Part I of the Step-by-Step Guide to prepare your project's Replication Recipe Pre-Registration file (see template here ). Request a review when your project is prepared; revise as necessary. Once approved by your local IRB, collect, analyze, and write up your data, including a completed data template (found within the files on this page; "CREP_nancekivell_data_template.xlsx") Follow Part II of your Step-by-Step Guide (includes creating a new version of your project and uploading your Replication Recipe Post-Completion  file [template here] ) Request another review when your completion files are posted; revise as necessary. Link both registrations in "Related Works" of your Zenodo project. Request a badge ; the CREP team will upload one to the top of your Zenodo project to indicate that you have completed the project lifecycle.   Replication Guidelines Original Materials to Use for Your Replication The original materials for the study can be found within "files."  Sample Size and Extensions Per CREP rules, collect the same N as the original; if the original N > 100, 100 participants is sufficient.  CREP can be flexible on N if participants are difficult to obtain at your institution. If your team runs a  Direct+ replication with additional survey items or within-participants conditions (e.g., running an additional set of statements), place added items  at the very end , after the seriousness check, so they cannot affect the exposure or truth-judgment phases.  If your team runs a Direct+ replication with additional between-participants conditions (e.g., an entirely different set of statements for one group), plan on running additional participants (100 for the direct replication and 100 more for each between-participants condition). Notes from the author No additional information was provided by the author.
items.title: CREP Replication of Study 1 from Nancekivell, Shah, & Gelman (2020)

items.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction. We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone. We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.
items.title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
